Trump has demanded that Volodymyr Zelenskyy stop attacking Russian oil refineries, claiming it is the cause of a global rise in the price of diesel fuel.
An attack on two neutral ships in Romanian territorial waters at the mouth of the Danube River indicated that strikes against vulnerable commercial targets are set to expand.
The Romanian president, Nicușor Dan, said two Russian drones violated Romanian airspace and struck two chemical tankers, setting the ships ablaze.
Rescue crews were searching for at least seven missing sailors.

He also attacked a gap in US intelligence sharing as “dangerous”.

items.title: France to go it alone on next-gen combat aircraft after FCAS collapse
items.originalTitle: France to go it alone on next-gen combat aircraft after FCAS collapse
items.summary: PARIS — France will develop a next-generation combat aircraft domestically as a successor to the Rafale, after a joint project with Germany and Spain for a future combat air system collapsed earlier this year, Air and Space Force Chief of Staff Jérôme Bellanger said. The country now conceives the future fighter, dubbed Avion de Combat du Futur or ACF, as a national project, with a target of flying conventional missions in 2040, Bellanger told the National Assembly’s defense committee in a hearing here on Wednesday.

evidenceRecords.text: PARIS — France will develop a next-generation combat aircraft domestically as a successor to the Rafale, after a joint project with Germany and Spain for a future combat air system collapsed earlier this year, Air and Space Force Chief of Staff Jérôme Bellanger said.

The country now conceives the future fighter, dubbed Avion de Combat du Futur or ACF, as a national project, with a target of flying conventional missions in 2040, Bellanger told the National Assembly’s defense committee in a hearing here on Wednesday.
“We’re now moving on to work that will prefigure and enable the birth of this ACF, this future combat aircraft as a national program,” Bellanger said.

France remains open to possible cooperation with other countries, “but within different frameworks and which won’t be structural to the birth of this aircraft.” France and Germany agreed to scrap the FCAS project in June, after years of wrangling about specifications and industrial control between Dassault Aviation and Airbus.

That’s left both countries without a clear successor for their existing fleets of Rafale and Eurofighter jets, respectively, though Germany has started receiving the first F-35 jets ordered in 2022 to replace the Panavia Tornado.

Dassault Aviation CEO Éric Trappier has said his company and France have all the know-how and skills to develop a next-generation fighter jet, together with engine partner Safran and defense-electronics firm Thales, and he would be able to do so “well below” a budget of €50 billion (US$56 billion).
All the years working on FCAS “haven’t been wasted,” with progress in areas including the aircraft, drones, stealth, connectivity and combat cloud, Bellanger said.
Work had been split up in several so-called pillars that also included a new engine, with Dassault and Airbus working on the next-gen fighter pillar at the heart of the system.
“The halt of the FCAS program doesn’t mean we’re throwing everything away,” Bellanger said.
“Our teams, the industrial teams have been working on the NGF, stealth, the cloud, and so on.

France will need to have a Rafale F5 standard in 2035 that incorporates the first components of the future combat aircraft, related to the engine, the sensors and the Stratus RS missile to neutralize enemy air defenses, according to Bellanger.

items.title: Power Up: Roll Out Solar Arrays Boost Space Station Power Supply
items.originalTitle: Power Up: Roll Out Solar Arrays Boost Space Station Power Supply
items.summary: 2 Min Read Power Up: Roll Out Solar Arrays Boost Space Station Power Supply From the International Space Station’s unique position 250 miles above Earth, the Sun is a vital source of energy. Solar power supports the station’s life support systems, daily activities, and hundreds of research investigations that improve life on Earth and prepare humans for deep space exploration. Over the past five years, NASA augmented the station’s power generation and distribution capability with next-generation International Space Station Roll Out Solar Arrays (IROSAs).

An International Space Station Roll Out Solar Array deploys in 2022.

Sunlight flares across the International Space Station’s solar arrays.

The first two International Space Station Roll Out Solar Arrays loaded in a SpaceX Dragon’s trunk before delivery to the orbiting laboratory during the company’s 22nd commercial resupply services mission for NASA in 2021.

In 2023, power projections prompted a request for another set of IROSAs, which launched in Dragon spacecraft’s trunk during the SpaceX 35th commercial resupply services mission to space station for NASA.

items.originalTitle: F-35C Begins Operational Testing Aboard Ford-Class Carrier John F. Kennedy
items.summary: The United States Navy has reached a significant milestone regarding the integration of the F-35C carrier-based variant of the Joint Strike Fighter on the Ford-class nuclear powered aircraft carriers. Beginning on October 13, F-35C “Lightning II” assigned to the “Salty Dogs” Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 23 based at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, embarked on PCU John F Kennedy (CVN-79) for aircraft launch and recovery operations.

evidenceRecords.text: The United States Navy has reached a significant milestone regarding the integration of the F-35C carrier-based variant of the Joint Strike Fighter on the Ford-class nuclear powered aircraft carriers.

Beginning on October 13, F-35C “Lightning II” assigned to the “Salty Dogs” Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 23 based at Naval Air Station Patuxent River, embarked on PCU John F Kennedy (CVN-79) for aircraft launch and recovery operations.
The US Navy released several sets of imagery detailing the arrival and operation of at least two F-35C, tail numbers 401 and 403 on the yet to be commissioned aircraft carrier.
The aircraft completed arrested recovery and catapult launches from CVN-79, utilising the carrier’s distinct EMALS and AAG electromagnetic launch and recovery systems.
Protracted integration of F-35C with newest US Navy carriers The first of class USS Gerald R.
However, to date the carrier does not embark F-35C, instead exclusively relying on air wings equipped with F/A-18E/F and G-variants for combat capability.
In contrast, US Navy F-35C have been operational on older Nimitz- class carriers for six years.
The first Nimitz -class carrier to operationally deploy the fighter jet was USS Carl Vinson in 2020, after initial testing with F-35C commencing on the carrier in 2017 .
A U.S. Navy F-35C Lightning II, attached to the “Salty Dogs” of Air Test and Evaluation Squadron (VX) 23, makes an arrested landing on the flight deck aboard PCU John F.
Kennedy (CVN 79), marking the first time an F-35C lands on a Ford-class aircraft carrier.

The principal reason for the delayed induction of F-35C with Ford -class carriers is the USN decision to extend various testing and integration measures on the new carrier-design as cost-saving measure, deriving from a Congress-mandated cost cap on the CVN-78-program.

In response the House Armed Services seapower and projection forces subcommittee in its FY2020 submission included language mandating that USN must not accept CVN-79 without the ability to embark the F-35C .

items.originalTitle: Honeywell Aerospace’s counter-drone software unites data from multiple sensors into one
items.summary: Counter-drone systems can combine radar, cameras, radio-frequency sensors and other equipment to detect, track and identify potential threats. Honeywell Aerospace’s SAMURAI system is designed to bring information from those disparate sources into a single interface. The system uses UNITAS, Honeywell Aerospace’s battle-management software, to integrate sensors and effectors from different manufacturers. “There is no one solution that solves every threat out there,” said retired Air Force Col. Tom Konicki, director of business at Honeywell Aerospace.

evidenceRecords.text: The system uses UNITAS , Honeywell Aerospace’s battle-management software, to integrate sensors and effectors from different manufacturers.
Tom Konicki, director of business at Honeywell Aerospace.
Konicki said counter-drone systems need to detect, track, identify, classify and ultimately defeat drones, regardless of the operator’s intent.

“There could be seven different sensors that have identified it and are feeding that into our software.” Konicki said the interface is designed to be straightforward for operators, including younger service members who may be assigned counter-drone duties without extensive experience operating the different systems.
He said Honeywell Aerospace has demonstrated the software to U.S. government and military representatives, as well as local law enforcement and state and city representatives.
The software also uses an open-architecture approach, allowing customers to integrate equipment they already own instead of replacing it with products from a single manufacturer.
Separately, Honeywell Aerospace announced Oct. 12 that its wholly owned subsidiary, EMS Defense Technologies, was selected for a Department of Homeland Security counter-drone contract vehicle .

Konicki said Honeywell Aerospace works with international partners, including Lithuania, Slovakia and Colombia, and can integrate locally sourced equipment when customers want to use particular sensors or effectors.

Honeywell Aerospace’s SAMURAI system is designed to bring information from those disparate sources into a single interface.
The system uses UNITAS, Honeywell Aerospace’s battle-management software, to integrate sensors and effectors from different manufacturers.
“There is no one solution that solves every threat out there,” said retired Air Force Col. Tom Konicki, director of business at Honeywell Aerospace.
The threat ranges from recreational drones flown into restricted airspace to unmanned aircraft that could be used to attack military installations or other critical infrastructure.
Konicki said operators of some counter-drone systems must monitor six, seven or eight separate screens for radar, cameras, radio-frequency sensors, jamming equipment and other capabilities.
That can require one operator to track multiple information streams simultaneously.
UNITAS is designed to consolidate the feeds so operators can view information from multiple sensors together in one interface.

items.title: Pentagon seeks expertise to develop brain injury assessment standards
items.originalTitle: Pentagon seeks expertise to develop brain injury assessment standards
items.summary: The Pentagon is looking to create standards to assess the impact of blast-induced mild traumatic brain injuries. The goal is to have benchmarks that will allow assessment of the “physiological and biomechanical effects of blast injuries” caused by explosions of enemy munitions or the blast effects from firing friendly weapons, according to the Request for Information by the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office, or BIRCO , within U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command .

evidenceRecords.text: The Pentagon is looking to create standards to assess the impact of blast-induced mild traumatic brain injuries.

The goal is to have benchmarks that will allow assessment of the “physiological and biomechanical effects of blast injuries” caused by explosions of enemy munitions or the blast effects from firing friendly weapons, according to the Request for Information by the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office, or BIRCO , within U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command .

This will enable “risk assessment of military service members who are exposed to blunt impacts resulting from acceleration of the body, blunt injury from a ballistic strike to the helmet, or effects from blast pressure produced by a weapon system or explosion,” the RFI reads.
BIRCO is seeking a variety of information that can help formulate standards for assessing mild traumatic brain injuries, or mTBI.
The information could include existing criteria, standards and models for brain injuries, as well as identifying experts on the topic.

The Pentagon is also seeking input from manufacturers of protective gear that can be “highly relevant to understanding human tolerance limits and predicting blast injuries.” The RFI uses a broad definition of blast injuries, including the effects on the body of blast-wave overpressure, fragments, the human body being thrown against hard objects, collapsing buildings and burns, as well as the effects of toxic gases and radiation.

“The standards can range from simple dose response curves and injury thresholds that address single components of blast insults, such as blast pressure wave magnitude, or address multiple components of blast insults, such as pressure magnitude over time,” the RFI said.

These standards will be used for “health hazard assessments, survivability assessments, and protection system development aimed at producing safe weapon systems, survivable combat platforms, and effective protection systems.” The effects of traumatic brain injuries on military personnel have become better known in recent years.

Partners and Khosla Ventures to accelerate the development and validation of its counter-swarm defense system.

The company’s system has been designed by Skapion’s Founding Architect, General (ret.) Pini Yungman, Architect of Iron Dome and former GM of Rafael Air & Missile Defense and engineered from inception around a native many-to-many architecture, enabling multiple interceptors to engage multiple targets simultaneously and at scale, said the company in a press release.

“The highly mobile, fully kinetic system is designed to simultaneously engage more than 100 targets with an interception rate above 97%, while delivering a significantly lower cost per interception compared with conventional air-defense solutions – creating an economically sustainable defense layer against mass, low-cost aerial threats,” said Skapion.
At the center of the system is an AI command-and-control architecture that fuses data from Skapion’s own detection and tracking sensors or third-party systems.
It evaluates and prioritizes threats, allocates interceptors and manages engagements in real time – allowing full end-to-end autonomy or a single human operator on the loop – per customer policy.
Skapion recently announced a USD36 million Seed funding round led by UP.
An open, sensor-agnostic architecture enables integration with external threat data, existing C2 systems and other counter-UAS systems.

evidenceRecords.text: Shield AI delivers the first V-BAT autonomous aircraft to the Taiwan Coast Guard Administration, enhancing maritime domain awareness with partner AIDC.

Shield AI press release Defense-tech company Shield AI announced the first delivery of its V-BAT to the Taiwan Coast Guard Administration (CGA) with its partner Aerospace Industrial Development Corporation (AIDC).
Shield AI’s V-BATs were competitively selected by the CGA in July 2026 for its “Shipborne UAV” program.
Shield AI engineers demonstrated aircraft setup within minutes, displaying V-BAT’s ease of operations and advanced technological capabilities for maritime security.
CGA will utilize V-BAT as a ship-based capability to maintain persistent Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) for surveillance, coastal patrols and law enforcement operations.
Vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) aircraft eliminate the need for runways and improve deployment flexibility while optimizing costs and reducing personnel requirements.
Partnering to build local expertise, Shield AI will train Coast Guard operators and maintenance personnel while simultaneously creating a robust localized support system for the V-BATs with AIDC.

“V-BAT will give Taiwan’s Coast Guard the maritime domain awareness and intelligence picture needed across the Taiwan Strait and its maritime borders,” said Brandon Tseng, Shield AI president and co-founder.
“V-BAT already does this for the U.S. Coast Guard, helping intercept more than 100,000 pounds of narcotics last year alone.
Extending those same capabilities to Taiwan helps keep the Strait safe from illegal activity and hostile actors.

It gives Taiwan the sovereignty it needs to protect its own waters.” Last year, Shield AI and AIDC entered into an agreement to advance Taiwan’s sovereign defense capabilities, strengthen its aerospace industrial base, and enhance collaborative technological innovation.

The companies have engaged in strategic collaboration through sustainment, training, autonomy integration, and other technical initiatives to ensure Shield AI’s products can be deployed, supported, and scaled in Taiwan.

items.originalTitle: Thales Australia tackles heavy battlefield logistics with new big-rig robot
items.summary: Thales Australia says it has built just such a robot. The company unveiled its BladeHaul extra-large, heavy-duty UGV on Oct. 6, the opening day of the Land Forces 2026 exhibition being held in Perth, Western Australia. Looking something akin to an aircraft tug, the BladeHaul relies on the chassis and driveline of Thales Australia’s popular Bushmaster 4x4 protected mobility vehicle that is in widespread Australian Army use.

evidenceRecords.text: Thales Australia says it has built just such a robot.
The company unveiled its BladeHaul extra-large, heavy-duty UGV on Oct. 6, the opening day of the Land Forces 2026 exhibition being held in Perth, Western Australia.

Looking something akin to an aircraft tug, the BladeHaul relies on the chassis and driveline of Thales Australia’s popular Bushmaster 4x4 protected mobility vehicle that is in widespread Australian Army use.

According to its designer, this uncrewed vehicle “is engineered to outperform all existing and planned counterparts in payload capacity and operational flexibility.” Official specs list a payload capacity of 10-plus tons for this cargo UGV, and a driving range comparable to that of the Bushmaster’s 600-plus kilometers.
The Bushmaster’s original mechanicals have been replaced by a hybrid energy and battery storage solution from 3ME Technology, Thales Australia’s partner in the effort.
For the BladeHaul the company has assembled a 660V power system that offers 110kWh of power.

Justin Bain, CEO of 3ME Technology, said: “Working with Thales Australia brings together the best of Australian innovation, combining 3ME Technology’s systems engineering and platform development capabilities with the Bushmaster’s proven performance and established manufacturing base.

Together we’re delivering an entirely new XL-UGV at a time when demand for contested logistics and remote power solutions for littoral environments is present and growing.” Thales Australia envisages three potential use cases for the BladeHaul: as a cargo mover in zones of contested logistics; as a mobile and enduring power source for other equipment; and as a highly mobile platform for sensors and effectors.

Thales Australia said in a statement: “By integrating advanced autonomy that enables human-machine teaming, hybrid technology, heavy payload capacity and power generation within a single platform, Thales Australia and 3ME Technology are delivering a next-generation solution that enhances operational readiness and supports Australia’s commitment to sovereign defense innovation.” The BladeHaul is aimed at the Australian Army, but its appeal extends to any land force, according to the manufacturer.

PRESS RELEASE — D-Wave Quantum Inc. (NASDAQ: QBTS) (“ D-Wave ” or the “Company”), the only dual-platform quantum computing company providing annealing and gate-model systems, software and services, today announced at Digital Innovation Forum 2026 that its Advantage2 TM annealing quantum computer has arrived in Lombardy, Italy, for installation at Villa Saporiti in Como.
The VoltaB1 Advantage2 annealing quantum computer will be formally inaugurated at Q-Alliance’s “ Quantum per l’Italia ” event on October 16, at the historic Villa Saporiti.
“Bringing Italy’s first annealing quantum computer to Como marks a historic milestone toward making quantum computing a working capability for Italian innovation and industry,” said Dr. Baratz.
That is how quantum infrastructure becomes industrial advantage.” The system’s arrival follows a €10 million agreement between D-Wave and SQT to deploy an annealing quantum computer in Europe.
Once operational, the Advantage2 system will be accessible through D – Wave’s Leap real-time quantum cloud service, which offers 99.9% availability and uptime.
“The arrival of the Advantage2 system in Lombardy puts physical infrastructure behind our vision for Italian quantum innovation,” said Thomas F.

“Our investment is intended to connect researchers and businesses with advanced computing resources, support the development of useful applications and help build the expertise that will sustain Italy’s role in the quantum economy.” Featuring more than 4,400 qubits, the Advantage2 system is D-Wave ’s most advanced annealing quantum computer and has demonstrated the ability to outperform classical computing on a complex materials simulation problem that would have taken one of the world’s most powerful classical supercomputers nearly one million years and the world’s annual electricity

Today, some of the world’s largest organizations across aviation, manufacturing, telecommunications and health care are using the Advantage2 system to address real-world problems, spanning optimization, materials simulation and artificial intelligence.

items.summary: Christopher Eubank on Monday at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington gave an approximate timeline for when the service would be delivering the new unit devoted to the exact same mission as the 11th Cyber Battalion, dubbed the Leviathans. “It should start standing up in earnest within the next couple months, and it will be an exact replica of the 11th Cyber Warfare Battalion,” Eubank said. The new battalion will achieve initial operating capability within the next year and from there work toward full operational capability, according to the Cyber Command leader.

evidenceRecords.text: Christopher Eubank on Monday at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington gave an approximate timeline for when the service would be delivering the new unit devoted to the exact same mission as the 11th Cyber Battalion, dubbed the Leviathans.
“It should start standing up in earnest within the next couple months, and it will be an exact replica of the 11th Cyber Warfare Battalion,” Eubank said.
The new battalion will achieve initial operating capability within the next year and from there work toward full operational capability, according to the Cyber Command leader.
The battalion is currently working on behalf of Joint Task Force–Southern Border, providing radio frequency-enabled cyber effects as directed by the division commander, Eubank said.
The Leviathans was activated on Oct. 16, 2022, as the first scalable expeditionary capability to handle the Army’s current and future cyberspace objectives.
Its previous iteration, the 915th Cyber Warfare Battalion, was activated on June 6, 2018, before being renamed during the 11th Cyber Battalion’s activation.
At the time of the battalion’s creation, the Army said it planned to have 12 expeditionary teams it could deploy under the 11th Cyber Battalion by September 2027.
The service has labeled the battalion the first of its kind.

Lou Etienne, who led the 11th Cyber Battalion until June 25.

Developers from 11th Cyber Command worked alongside the Cyber Solutions Development unit within the 780th Military Intelligence Brigade to develop new drone technology between July 2025 and July 2026.

The partnership project was performed to support the Army’s “Transforming in Contact” initiative, which delivers new unmanned technology to soldiers to track their feedback in real time as they utilize it in the field.

items.title: How ADI is helping robotics startups scale
items.originalTitle: How ADI is helping robotics startups scale
items.summary: “The biggest challenge I see robotics startups facing today is the speed at which the industry moves,” says Cameron Villone, Senior Product Technology Manager at Analog Devices Inc. (ADI). In most cases, a startup excels in adopting next-generation technologies in sensing, motion control, and AI, but commercialization requires additional expertise in electronics, system integration, validation, and manufacturing. These demands can often stretch the resources of smaller engineering teams.

evidenceRecords.text: “The biggest challenge I see robotics startups facing today is the speed at which the industry moves,” says Cameron Villone, Senior Product Technology Manager at Analog Devices Inc. (ADI).

In most cases, a startup excels in adopting next-generation technologies in sensing, motion control, and AI, but commercialization requires additional expertise in electronics, system integration, validation, and manufacturing.
These demands can often stretch the resources of smaller engineering teams.
ADI is developing its Emerging Tech Hub within the Analog Garage to help robotics startups and established companies overcome these challenges.
The Emerging Tech Hub is intended to give companies access to ADI engineers, prototyping and testing resources, and manufacturing and sourcing expertise as they prepare their designs for production.

The challenges of scaling robotics innovation ADI was recently highlighted in The Race to Make AI Physical whitepaper explaining how physical AI brings together sensing, signal conversion, perception, reasoning, control, computing, and validation.
ADI describes this through four stages: Idea, Prototype, Validate, and Scale.
These changing demands for a robotics startup are the gaps ADI’s Emerging Tech Hub is intended to address.

The Emerging Tech Hub brings expertise and resources The Emerging Tech Hub is a robotics-focused initiative being developed to bring startups and established robotics companies closer to ADI’s technical teams, including engineers implementing newly released or still-in-development technologies.
The engineering support from ADI will depend on the robotics company’s stage and needs.

For example, a mature robotics developer might need a particular semiconductor component, while another may be trying to solve a different engineering problem, prompting the Emerging Tech Hub to find specialists within ADI.
Villone said ADI has recruited robotics experts from across the industry to be better equipped to handle fast paced robotic development.

items.title: Dirac Labs joins Wisconsin Security Research Consortium
items.originalTitle: Dirac Labs joins Wisconsin Security Research Consortium
items.summary: Insider Brief Dirac Labs has joined the Wisconsin Security Research Consortium as an industry affiliate to advance GPS-independent quantum navigation for autonomous maritime missions. The Madison-based company is developing diamond-based magnetic sensors and AI processing to determine position underwater, underground and where GPS is disrupted or unavailable. The affiliation connects Dirac Labs with Wisconsin’s defense research network and supports Area 52, a proposed Lake Michigan testing ground for autonomous maritime systems.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Dirac Labs has joined the Wisconsin Security Research Consortium as an industry affiliate to advance GPS-independent quantum navigation for autonomous maritime missions.
The Madison-based company is developing diamond-based magnetic sensors and AI processing to determine position underwater, underground and where GPS is disrupted or unavailable.
The affiliation connects Dirac Labs with Wisconsin’s defense research network and supports Area 52, a proposed Lake Michigan testing ground for autonomous maritime systems.

PRESS RELEASE — Dirac Labs, a Madison-based quantum-enabled navigation company, today announced that it has joined the Wisconsin Security Research Consortium (WSRC) as an industry affiliate, providing resilient navigation alternatives to enable autonomous maritime missions.

WSRC, led by the Wisconsin Technology Council, connects Wisconsin’s universities, technology manufacturers and government partners to advance defense research and economic development opportunities in the state.

Dirac Labs’ affiliation builds on the Autonomous Heartland effort to position Wisconsin — with its shipyards, airspace, industrial base, workforce, and research anchors — at the center of America’s autonomous and maritime future.
Along with the Sagamore Institute, the Midwest Defense Accelerator and TitletownTech, WSRC supports the growing Area 52 initiative.
Area 52 was originally proposed by retired U.S. Navy captain Jerry Hendrix to serve as the Navy’s equivalent to the Air Force’s Area 51.

Lake Michigan is a uniquely suitable option, as it is the only Great Lake entirely within U.S. territory that is large and deep enough for both surface and subsurface testing, and it has existing FAA-designated restricted military airspace overhead connected to assets like Volk Field.
Dirac Labs is building a quantum universal positioning system designed to work underwater, underground and in environments where GPS is contested.
“Dirac Labs is rooted in UW–Madison research, focused on a hard national security problem, and building technology designed to be manufactured at scale.
It gives us a direct path to move our sensors from prototypes to the field, with Wisconsin partners alongside us.” To learn more about Dirac Labs, please visit diraclabs.com .

items.originalTitle: IonQ and University of Cambridge Open Quantum Innovation Centre
items.summary: Insider Brief IonQ and the University of Cambridge have opened the IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre at the Ray Dolby Centre, establishing the company’s first university-based centre of this kind. The centre’s nine initial research projects will cover quantum networking, sensing, hardware development and applications in fields including chemistry, materials science, finance, engineering and medicine.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief IonQ and the University of Cambridge have opened the IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre at the Ray Dolby Centre, establishing the company’s first university-based centre of this kind.

The centre’s nine initial research projects will cover quantum networking, sensing, hardware development and applications in fields including chemistry, materials science, finance, engineering and medicine.

IonQ plans to deploy a 256-qubit Superion quantum computer and an on-campus quantum network, while Innovate UK will provide the National Quantum Computing Centre with access and computing time over three years.

PRESS RELEASE — IonQ (NYSE: IONQ), the world’s leading full-stack quantum platform and foundry, and the University of Cambridge have announced the opening of the first-ever university-based IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre.
The Centre is located at the Ray Dolby Centre, the new home of the University’s Cavendish Laboratory.
The IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre demonstrates the company’s commitment to quantum innovation and academic research within the United Kingdom.
Research at the Centre includes co-development of new quantum network nodes and sensing capabilities with the university, and a strengthening of the existing Cambridge-to-Bristol quantum network.
IonQ and the University of Cambridge first announced the partnership on March 11, 2026, supporting advanced research and workforce development for quantum technologies.

“The opening of the IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre turns a landmark agreement into a working home for quantum research inside one of the world’s most storied physics laboratories,” said Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ.

This is a long-term commitment to the United Kingdom, built for researchers, start-ups, and industry alike.” The Centre’s nine inaugural research projects will bring together Cambridge researchers and IonQ specialists to advance quantum hardware and explore new applications across science and industry.

Selected by a Joint Steering Committee comprising business and scientific leaders from both organizations, the projects combine Cambridge’s research expertise with IonQ’s capabilities in trapped-ion quantum computing, quantum networking, and device engineering.

“The official launch of the IonQ Quantum Innovation Centre is an exciting milestone in our partnership with IonQ, which will help Cambridge and the UK stay at the forefront of the quantum revolution,” said Professor Mete Atatüre, Head of the Cavendish Laboratory.

items.originalTitle: SEALSQ Reports 65% Revenue Growth in First Nine Months of 2026
items.summary: Insider Brief SEALSQ reported preliminary nine-month 2026 revenue of $16.3 million, up 65% year over year, and reaffirmed its full-year revenue guidance of $27 million to $36 million. SEALSQ said 42 prospective customers and partners were evaluating its QS7001 and QVault TPM products, with additional certification milestones and broader post-quantum revenue contributions expected in 2027 and beyond.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief SEALSQ reported preliminary nine-month 2026 revenue of $16.3 million, up 65% year over year, and reaffirmed its full-year revenue guidance of $27 million to $36 million.

SEALSQ said 42 prospective customers and partners were evaluating its QS7001 and QVault TPM products, with additional certification milestones and broader post-quantum revenue contributions expected in 2027 and beyond.

PRESS RELEASE — SEALSQ Corp (NASDAQ: LAES) (“SEALSQ” or “Company”), a company that focuses on developing and selling Semiconductors, PKI, and Post-Quantum technology hardware and software products, today announced its preliminary unaudited financial metrics for the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026 (“9M 2026”), provided an update on operational milestones, and reaffirmed its full-year 2026 revenue guidance.
9M 2026 Key Financial Metrics Revenue growth of 65%: Preliminary unaudited 9M 2026 revenue of $16.3 million, compared to $9.9 million in 9M 2025.

Revenue Drivers The 9M 2026 increase was driven primarily by: Continued strong demand for SEALSQ ‘s Vault-IC secure-element family across industrial, smart-energy IoT and P25 Radio protocol application deployments.
Nine months of consolidated revenue from IC’Alps SAS, which contributed approximately $3.8 million in 9M 2026 through custom ASIC design and secure semiconductor engineering services.
FY 2026 Revenue Outlook SEALSQ ‘s outlook statements are based on current expectations.

SEALSQ reaffirms its FY 2026 revenue growth guidance of approximately 50% to 100%, representing a range of approximately $27 million to $36 million, compared with audited FY 2025 revenue of $18 million.
Seasonal strength in Vault-IC secure-element shipments and continued growth in recurring PKI and certificate-management revenue.

Carlos Moreira, Founder, Chairman and CEO of SEALSQ , said: “Our preliminary nine-month revenue of $16.3 million represents 65% growth year-over-year, with revenue increasing sequentially in each quarter of 2026.

With approximately $465 million in liquidity, we are well positioned to fund these priorities as we prepare for post-quantum semiconductors to become a more significant contributor to revenue in 2027.” John O’Hara, CFO of SEALSQ , added: “Based on our preliminary nine-month revenue, our reaffirmed full-year 2026 revenue guidance implies fourth-quarter revenue of $11 million to $20 million.

We remain focused on converting our pipeline into production revenue and deploying capital carefully to support growth.” Post-Quantum Commercialization and Certification Progress QS7001: Following fault-injection and side-channel testing (March 2026) and NIST SP 800-90B Entropy Source Validation, Certificate #E333 (May 2026), SEALSQ targets the QS7001 V1 Common Criteria Hardware Evaluation Test Report in October 2026 and the V2 full post-quantum report in January 2027, with formal CC EAL5+ certification progressing in 2027.

evidenceRecords.text: With both solid rocket boosters fully stacked and all four RS-25 engines now installed on the Core Stage, NASA is preparing to mate the stage to the boosters and form the short stack that will roll to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test.
The test, expected in the coming months, will also give the Artemis III crew their first full launch-day rehearsal on the pad ahead of the targeted no-earlier-than June 2027 mission.

Engineers with NASA’s Exploration Ground Systems finished stacking the twin five-segment boosters on September 30 by mating the aerodynamic nose cones to the left and right forward assemblies inside the Vehicle Assembly Building’s High Bay 3 at Kennedy Space Center.
The boosters, built by Northrop Grumman, will deliver more than 75 percent of total SLS thrust at liftoff from Pad 39B.
NASA plans to roll the short stack to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test, during which the launch team will practice propellant loading timelines and procedures.

items.originalTitle: France mulls keeping Charles de Gaulle carrier sailing after 2038
items.summary: PARIS — France is studying whether the Charles de Gaulle nuclear-powered aircraft carrier can continue to sail beyond its envisaged retirement in 2038, which would give the country a fleet of two carriers, French Navy Chief of Staff Adm. Christophe Cluzel told lawmakers in a hearing here on Wednesday. The French Navy plans to replace the Charles de Gaulle, the only nuclear-powered aircraft carrier in operation outside the United States Navy, with a future carrier to be named France Libre in 2038.

evidenceRecords.text: PARIS — France is studying whether the Charles de Gaulle nuclear-powered aircraft carrier can continue to sail beyond its envisaged retirement in 2038, which would give the country a fleet of two carriers, French Navy Chief of Staff Adm.
Christophe Cluzel told lawmakers in a hearing here on Wednesday.
The French Navy plans to replace the Charles de Gaulle, the only nuclear-powered aircraft carrier in operation outside the United States Navy, with a future carrier to be named France Libre in 2038.
As part of an upcoming major refit, France will look into whether the Charles de Gaulle can continue to operate longer, based on the state of onboard systems and the nuclear propulsion, Cluzel said.

With a single carrier, France is without one any time the Charles de Gaulle is in dock for periodic maintenance, and the issue of whether the country needs a second carrier tends to pop up whenever lawmakers question Navy brass.
One obstacle is cost, with the estimated €10 billion budget (US$11.2 billion) for the future France Libre carrier enough to fund at least ten new FDI-class frigates.
Two carriers allow you to maintain a standing alert from Toulon,” Cluzel told the National Assembly’s defense committee, referring to the Charles de Gaulle’s home port in southern France.

He said the future France Libre and the Charles de Gaulle will have two years of overlap in 2036-2038, with two aircraft-carrier crews on active duty, which the Navy chief said is necessary for a seamless transition of skills.

“So from 2036 to 2038 there is a period when the Navy will again have two carriers able to be at sea simultaneously. ”France has said the France Libre will measure 310 meters and displace about 80,000 tonnes, compared to 261.5 meters and 42,000 tons for the Charles de Gaulle.

Studies on extending the Charles de Gaulle’s service life will look at the wear on the reactor cores at the heart of the carrier’s nuclear propulsion system, and the ability to extend operations by keeping fuel on board the carrier for longer, according to Cluzel.

France is committed to limiting its dependencies, and similar to what it did for the steam-powered catapults on the Charles de Gaulle, the country will buy a “substantial” inventory of spare parts for its electromagnetic catapults right at the start of the program, to ensure it can perform repairs independently, according to Cluzel.

items.originalTitle: Quantum Alliance Launches to Set Post-Quantum Standards for Blockchains
items.summary: Insider Brief Leaders from nine blockchain organizations have launched the Quantum Alliance , an open standards initiative to define and verify post-quantum readiness across blockchain networks, wallets and infrastructure. The Alliance plans to publish open testing criteria, benchmarks and migration guidance covering transaction signatures, key management, consensus, zero-knowledge proofs and peer-to-peer connections. Its initial work will focus on four areas: blockchain migration, post-quantum zero-knowledge systems, wallet security and cross-chain compatibility.

The Alliance plans to publish open testing criteria, benchmarks and migration guidance covering transaction signatures, key management, consensus, zero-knowledge proofs and peer-to-peer connections.
Its initial work will focus on four areas: blockchain migration, post-quantum zero-knowledge systems, wallet security and cross-chain compatibility.

PRESS RELEASE — CEOs, CTOs, and founders from nine blockchain organizations today launched the Quantum Alliance , an open standards body that will set the criteria for judging quantum-resistance claims in blockchain and create standards for compatibility between the networks as they migrate.
The Alliance will define what post-quantum readiness means for blockchain networks, wallets, and infrastructure, and how to test and verify any claim of quantum resistance.

Nearly every major blockchain secures its accounts with elliptic-curve signatures, and once an account signs a transaction (for some address types, from the moment it is created), its public key sits permanently on a public ledger.
A sufficiently capable quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm could work backward from that public key to the private key and take control of the funds.
The same signatures protect stablecoin minting keys, governance contracts, bridges, and oracle feeds, so one compromised privileged key could spread across many platforms at once.
The Quantum Alliance was formed to set that bar.

evidenceRecords.text: Türkiye’s domestically developed MALAMAN smart bottom mine was deployed during the multinational Nusret 2026 mine warfare exercise, marking another operational milestone for the system.
Hosted by Türkiye from October 6 to 16 in the Gulf of Izmir and off Karadeniz Ereğli in the Black Sea, the Nusret 2026 Invitation Exercise provided the operational backdrop for the demonstration.
During the exercise, a MALAMAN mine was seen being laid from the Turkish Navy’s Tuzla-class patrol boat TCG Karabiga (P-1205).
Wrapped in artificial grass camouflage designed to mimic seabed vegetation, the mine was launched into the water from the ship’s stern.
MALAMAN was developed through a joint defense industry effort involving KoçSavunma, MKE, and TÜBİTAK SAGE to address the Turkish Navy’s modern mine warfare requirements.
According to details released by the Turkish Ministry of National Defence, Nusret 2026 brings together 20 naval vessels, five aircraft, and various unmanned systems.
Turkish Naval Forces, Air Force, and Coast Guard units are participating alongside NATO and partner nations.

Key participant groups include NATO’s Standing Mine Countermeasures Group 2 (SNMCMG2)—with assets from Germany, Greece, Italy, Spain, and Türkiye—and the Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Task Group, featuring ships from Bulgaria, Romania, and Türkiye.
The exercise focuses on the planning, execution, and evaluation of mine warfare operations, emphasizing interoperability in multi-threat environments.

About the MALAMAN Smart Mine A mockup of Malaman Smart Sea Mine exhibited at DSA 2024 in Malaysia MALAMAN is a seabed/bottom mine equipped with acoustic, magnetic and pressure sensors for target detection and classification.

Building on this open ecosystem, researchers can build agentic reasoning capabilities with NVIDIA Nemotron — a family of architectures, open weights, open source models, training data and recipes — and scientific software including NVIDIA BioNeMo Agent Toolkit , NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo libraries, NVIDIA Earth-2 models and NVIDIA ALCHEMI NIM microservices to accelerate research across biology, chemistry, molecular design, weather and climate, energy, engineering, physics and material sciences.
Skills and Training Building advanced intelligence capability across Europe requires knowledge that travels as freely as compute.

The NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute has launched a new open source courseware hub with hands-on course materials covering accelerated computing and deep learning — freely downloadable and openly licensed, with no enrollment, fees or deadline.

Modular by design, the courses can be adapted for university curricula, supercomputing center bootcamps or developer community events, and serve as a direct bridge to NVIDIA’s broader training and certification programs .

items.title: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance
items.originalTitle: Rigorous Analysis Confirms NASA’s Artemis II Heat Shield Performance
items.summary: Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected. After NASA’s thorough analysis of Artemis I heat shield findings , informed by extensive arc jet material testing at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley, the agency modified Orion’s reentry trajectory for Artemis II by shortening the maximum downrange distance the spacecraft could fly between when it entered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.

evidenceRecords.text: Additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed initial data showing the heat shield performed as expected.

After NASA’s thorough analysis of Artemis I heat shield findings , informed by extensive arc jet material testing at NASA’s Ames Research Center in California’s Silicon Valley, the agency modified Orion’s reentry trajectory for Artemis II by shortening the maximum downrange distance the spacecraft could fly between when it entered Earth’s atmosphere and splashed down in the Pacific Ocean.

Analysis prior to the mission showed that limiting downrange distance would limit how long the spacecraft’s heat shield spent in the temperature range at which the Artemis I heat shield phenomenon occurred.
Shortly after Artemis II splashdown on April 10, 2026, U.S. Navy divers captured underwater imagery of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield.

Initial inspections of the thermal protection system, including diver imagery of the spacecraft’s heat shield taken just after splashdown and further inspections on the recovery ship, found it performed as expected, with a significant reduction in the amount of cracks and char loss as compared to Artemis I.

Upon the spacecraft’s return to NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida after the Moon mission, thermal protection system experts began additional examination of the heat shield, made of 186 unique blocks of an ablative material called Avcoat.

The heat shield was then transported to NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, where work on sample extraction and internal x-ray scans began in August to provide further engineering insight into the system and behavior of the material.

NASA/Kevin Davis A thorough post-flight assessment review found that Orion’s aerodynamic and aerothermal performance, including the heat shield and backshell thermal protection system, was in line with engineering predictions based on pre-flight analyses and ground testing.

The shorter allowable down range during entry reduced the cracking and char loss experienced on the Artemis II heat shield relative to the Artemis I heat shield by a factor of ten, proving the effectiveness of the trajectory modification.
Engineers found only nine spots of char loss of varying sizes on the Artemis II heat shield dish, compared to 103 during Artemis I.

The analysis also showed that Orion’s robust heat shield design showed consistency from Artemis I to Artemis II, evident by the performance of system features such as the seams between the heat shield Avcoat blocks and the Avcoat surrounding the heat shield compression pad separation bolts.

The team also performed post-flight laser scans of the heat shield surface and is comparing this data to pre-flight measurements to determine material recession, which will then be compared to analysis predictions.

“The end state is economic supremacy for the United States,” Ryan said, later adding, “We have ceded control of that economic terrain in this hemisphere to the People’s Republic of China over at least the last two decades, and that is a major threat to our national security.” Ryan pointed to Panama as an example, explaining how a high percentage of trade to and from the United States passes through the Panama Canal.

Ryan said the task force would receive more rotary-wing aircraft and personnel to “address some of the natural disasters and threats in the region.” Those additional resources, he said, “become absolutely critical when you’re talking about moving supplies, moving people to the point of need, and making assessments.” Command restructure In a major force restructure, the Army stood up the Western Hemisphere Command in December 2025, combining U.S. Army North, U.S. Army South and Armed Forces Command under a single headquarters.

evidenceRecords.text: HII announced that its Newport News Shipbuilding (NNS) division was awarded a $56 million contract by the U.S. Navy for shipbuilding engineering and design in support of the trilateral Australia, United Kingdom, and United States (AUKUS) partnership.
HII press release The contract includes an option which, if exercised, would bring the cumulative value of this contract to $91 million.
HII continues to take a whole-company approach to support the AUKUS agreement, providing services and support for AUKUS across its business divisions.

Under the contract, in support of Foreign Military Sales (FMS) requirements, NNS will continue supporting the United Kingdom and Australia, including technology insertion, engineering, supply chain and workforce development support, and digital transformation.

The award also includes the United States Industry Support (USIS) effort, wherein NNS engineers and designers will support the design of the SSN-AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine to be built by the United Kingdom and Australia.
“Our longstanding nuclear experience at NNS directly benefits the AUKUS mission to support shared security objectives,” said Bryan Caccavale, NNS vice president of program management.

“We are honored to leverage that experience and contribute even more to the AUKUS partnership.” The contract award is the latest in a range of initiatives HII is actively engaged in to advance the AUKUS partnership.

HII’s Mission Technologies division in Australia was awarded the contract to deliver the Australian Submarine Supplier Qualification (AUSSQ) Program , which accelerates the identification, development and qualification of Australian suppliers for integration into the United States submarine industrial base.
HII is also working with Australian industry and academia in Australia to develop the skilled workforce needed to support Australia’s nuclear-powered submarine enterprise.

The company was also awarded the Australian Submarine Agency’s Nuclear Capability Advisory Services (ANCAS) contract in December 2025 to support development of Australia’s Nuclear Power Submarine (NPS) programs through nuclear program management and technical support services. – End –

evidenceRecords.text: ANRA Technologies has introduced VISTA (Visual Interface for Shared Traffic Awareness), an application designed to give public safety agencies and commercial drone operators greater awareness of nearby drone activity through information available from UAS traffic management (UTM) services.
The application displays available flight intentions and reported positions, helping operators understand what other aircraft may be operating nearby before and during a mission.
It does not require changes to existing drones, flight applications or operating procedures.
VISTA is designed to complement existing safety procedures rather than detect every drone in the sky.

The receive-only application does not connect aircraft to UTM services or submit flight plans, instead providing an additional layer of airspace awareness based on information available through the UTM ecosystem.

ANRA said its UTM platform supports approximately one drone mission every 15 seconds during daytime operations, while more than 20 organisations, primarily Drone as First Responder (DFR) programmes, already use its visualisation capabilities.
The company said VISTA is intended to help public safety agencies coordinate drone operations near emergency scenes, while also supporting enterprise activities such as infrastructure inspections.
ANRA is offering demonstrations to organisations interested in the application.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief EMode Photonix raised $1 million in pre-seed funding led by Ground State Ventures , with participation from Harlow Capital Management, to expand its photonics simulation software business.
The company says its software simulates nonlinear photonic circuits 1,000 times faster, helping engineers design devices for frequency conversion and quantum light generation.
The Boulder-based startup will use the funding to expand product development and sales as it prepares an enterprise offering for complete photonic integrated circuit design.

PRESS RELEASE — EMode Photonix ( EMode , Inc.), a startup delivering powerful simulation tools to allow novel photonics technologies for quantum computers to be developed faster, has raised a $1 million pre-seed round.
The round was led by Ground State Ventures , with participation from Harlow Capital Management.

Traditionally developed for telecommunications, it is finding increasing use in sensing, computing (see Nvidia investing billions in partnerships with photonics companies to replace copper wire), and especially quantum technologies.
Traditionally photonics engineers could rely on existing simulations of linear photonics, which is sufficient for simple light routing circuits.

However, the next generation of photonic devices exploit non-linear photonics, which not only allows one to bridge and generate different frequencies of light, but even enables the conversion of classical to quantum light.
Up until now, there haven’t been any efficient tools for simulating non-linear photonics.
EMode Photonix has developed a unique simulation stack, based on proprietary computational techniques, that speeds up the simulation of non-linear photonic circuits by 1,000x.

“We’re excited to be building a foundational tool for the next generation of photonic engineering and technology.” EMode Photonix ’s advanced photonics simulation software is specifically designed to model and optimize complex light transformations.

The software incorporates newly derived equations for frequency conversion together with other physics like thermal and RF, enabling engineers to design devices that transform light from one color to another, or from classical light into quantum light.

items.originalTitle: Ukraine resumes attacks on Russian refineries as Zelenskyy says 'we're done'

evidenceRecords.text: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has announced that Ukraine is resuming attacks on Russian energy sites.

Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, on Thursday said that his country's military had resumed strikes on Russian energy infrastructure despite US President Donald Trump's insistence that such attacks stop.
Zelenskyy made the statement in an interview with London's Financial Times (FT) newspaper, saying: "The block [on energy infrastructure attacks] is out.
We're done."
Kyiv had refrained from making attacks to give Trump's "energy ceasefire" a chance for success.

On Thursday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov praised "vigorous [US] efforts to initiate the peace process," and claimed that by resuming attacks, Ukraine "is coming into serious conflict with the peace efforts of the United States and American negotiators."

Russia, however, has paid no heed to Trump, instead continuing to hit Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure, for instance on Wednesday, when Russian strikes cut power to 600,000 Ukrainian citizens.
Ukraine had gone along with Trump's public proposal — despite not being notified of any "ceasefire" ahead of time — but it seemed to have helped little in the eyes of US leadership.

To that end, Zelenskyy railed against a "dangerous" lack of US intelligence information this week as well as the throttling of SpaceX Starlink satellite access for Ukraine's troops after Trump last week announced a number of decisions that have had adverse consequences for Ukraine.
The Ukrainian president said his country's military leaders had been warned that they would not be receiving US intelligence if they did not abide by Trump's "ceasefire."
Despite Ukraine's restraint, that withholding of intelligence was on full display this week when Kyiv was blindsided by Russian drones and missiles without any prior warning from the US.
"We will find a way out," said Zelenskyy of the situation as Ukraine's Western allies scramble to pick up the intelligence and defensive slack left by the US.

Zelenskyy said he would be willing to halt energy infrastructure attacks again but only if the US supplied Patriot interceptors that would allow Kyiv to down incoming the Russian ballistic missiles and drones that have been raining down on Ukraine since February 24, 2022.
Despite US claims that the Starlink situation was the result of a technical glitch, Zelenskyy told the FT, "It was not a technical problem, it was will."

items.title: Riverlane and NVIDIA Use AI to Speed Up Quantum Decoder Calibration
items.originalTitle: Riverlane and NVIDIA Use AI to Speed Up Quantum Decoder Calibration
items.summary: Insider Brief Riverlane and NVIDIA are exploring how AI and GPU-accelerated computing can speed up decoder calibration for quantum error correction as quantum hardware behaviour changes. Using Riverlane ’s Local Clustering Decoder on an NVIDIA H100 GPU, the reported surface-code training cycle fell from three minutes on a single CPU core to 2.8 seconds. The H100 processed more than four million surface-code syndromes per second in the reported tests, compared with around 59,000 per second on a single CPU core, supporting more frequent decoder recalibration.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Riverlane and NVIDIA are exploring how AI and GPU-accelerated computing can speed up decoder calibration for quantum error correction as quantum hardware behaviour changes.
Using Riverlane ’s Local Clustering Decoder on an NVIDIA H100 GPU, the reported surface-code training cycle fell from three minutes on a single CPU core to 2.8 seconds.

The H100 processed more than four million surface-code syndromes per second in the reported tests, compared with around 59,000 per second on a single CPU core, supporting more frequent decoder recalibration.
PRESS RELEASE — Quantum computing has the potential to solve problems beyond the reach of today’s computers, from drug discovery to materials science and optimisation.
But before that can happen, the industry must first overcome the errors that are created by quantum computing’s extreme sensitivity to noise.
Quantum error correction (QEC) detects and corrects these errors.
It’s essential for building reliable and useful quantum computers, but this also creates enormous demands for real-time data processing.
Future systems may need to process terabytes of information every second, with near-perfect accuracy, to support error-free quantum computing.

To explore how to meet these demands, Riverlane and NVIDIA are collaborating on the use of AI and NVIDIA accelerated computing for QEC, including how GPUs can make decoder calibration faster, and help quantum systems keep up with changes in hardware behaviour.
Keeping up with Changing Quantum Hardware A decoder is the part of a QEC system that interprets the signals produced by a quantum processor.
Building a Faster and More Efficient Calibration Loop Riverlane has developed an AI-based calibration loop that learns improved decoder settings directly from experimental data.
As part of a collaboration, Riverlane uses NVIDIA H100 GPU to test how well different decoder settings perform.

items.title: US soldiers must train on ‘new basics’ of unmanned systems, officials say
items.originalTitle: US soldiers must train on ‘new basics’ of unmanned systems, officials say
items.summary: Within the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, or 2CR, new basics include unmanned aerial systems operation and employment, counter-UAS systems and unmanned ground vehicle usage, service officials said during a Monday discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting , titled “ Project Flytrap —Accelerating Offensive Maneuver through Data-Centric Kill Web.” Project Flytrap is an Army counter-unmanned aerial systems initiative and multinational exercise, which has leveled up from the individual soldier to the squadron level with multiple iterations.

evidenceRecords.text: Within the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, or 2CR, new basics include unmanned aerial systems operation and employment, counter-UAS systems and unmanned ground vehicle usage, service officials said during a Monday discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting , titled “ Project Flytrap —Accelerating Offensive Maneuver through Data-Centric Kill Web.” Project Flytrap is an Army counter-unmanned aerial systems initiative and multinational exercise, which has leveled up from the individual soldier to the squadron level with multiple iterations.

The most recent exercise, Project Flytrap 5.0, took place in Lithuania and was concluded earlier this year with partner nations, including the United Kingdom and Australia, and was led by the Army’s V Corps .
The countries integrated and tested more than 50 industry-provided technologies, launched effects and unmanned ground vehicles and tested against a live opposing force.
“The American way of war is centered on maneuver, and counter-UAS cannot remain tied to static defense,” Col.
Timothy Price, commander of the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, said in a Tuesday release .

“Project FlyTrap ensures we maintain mobility and offensive survivability in a highly contested, opaque operational environment.” The 2nd Cavalry Regiment is expanding Project Flytrap into a battalion-level operational capability, adapting from small-unit field trials into tactical employment connected with operational objectives aimed at breaking through drone-saturated frontlines on Europe’s Eastern Flank.
“As we’re training our soldiers for the multi-domain operations, or multi-domain breeds, we talk about the new basics inside of 2CR,” Command Sgt.
Jesse Clark, 2nd Cavalry Regiment senior enlisted leader, said during Monday’s discussion.

“With the new basics, we need to focus on sUAS, counter-UAS, camouflage for electromagnetic signatures … and how we’re going to do that so soldiers understand how to camouflage themselves with those spectrum options,” he continued.
Officials listed the previous basics to include topics such as marksmanship, map reading and navigation, radio etiquette and UAS and jamming reaction to contact.
Clark said the service needs to have disciplined unit training management in which personnel, time and equipment are included to ensure soldiers are proficient at the new basics.

items.title: The Download: reviving frozen pig kidneys and boosting nuclear power
items.originalTitle: The Download: reviving frozen pig kidneys and boosting nuclear power
items.summary: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists. The kidneys, which are similar in size to human ones, were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year. Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working.

items.title: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
items.originalTitle: Trump calls off livestream of Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad
items.summary: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad. Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it. Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally. On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".

evidenceRecords.text: US President Donald Trump has called off plans to livestream the execution of former US army psychiatrist Nidal Hasan by firing squad.
Trump had previously said he approved of showing the death of the Fort Hood attacker, while Vice-President JD Vance cast doubt on whether it would happen and said he would not watch it.
Trump's decision to cancel the livestream came after widespread criticism in the US and globally.
On Thursday, he said that "many very good and well meaning people would rather not watch him die".
"I think streaming the execution for all to see might have been a strong deterrent for the World to witness how America deals with Terrorists and SCUM like Hasan," Trump said.
"He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," the president added.
Hasan fatally shot 13 unarmed US soldiers at a military base in Texas in 2009, injuring another 32.
His execution by firing squad will be the first military execution in more than 60 years.
Trump said the families of the victims can still view the execution in person if they wish.

After the Pentagon announced last week that it would execute Hasan on 3 December 2026 by firing squad and livestream the event, a cascade of criticism quickly followed from human rights groups and many others.
The United Nations called the plans "abhorrent".
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth defended his decision to air Hasan's execution online, saying that "people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things".

But as criticism mounted, Trump appeared to hedge his support, saying on Friday that he "absolutely" approved of the livestream plan, but adding that the Pentagon was still "making a determination" on it.
The president also called Hasan "totally nuts".
John Galligan, a lawyer for Hasan working primarily on civil issues, told the BBC that Trump's decision to cancel the livestream of his execution "comes as no surprise".

items.title: CASA to continue broad-area BVLOS trial as long-term guidance is developed
items.originalTitle: CASA to continue broad-area BVLOS trial as long-term guidance is developed
items.summary: Australia’s Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) will continue its broad-area beyond visual line-of-sight (BVLOS) drone trial while developing a long-term approach to these operations. Following an internal review, CASA is working on an enduring framework that builds on the existing trial arrangements, which provide eligible operators with more flexible pathways to conduct BVLOS flights across larger areas. The regulator expects to open public consultation in November 2026 on draft guidance for broad-area BVLOS operations.

Following an internal review, CASA is working on an enduring framework that builds on the existing trial arrangements, which provide eligible operators with more flexible pathways to conduct BVLOS flights across larger areas.
The regulator expects to open public consultation in November 2026 on draft guidance for broad-area BVLOS operations.
CASA will seek industry feedback to ensure the guidance is clear and practical for operators applying for broad-area BVLOS approvals.
Existing trial arrangements will remain in place until a long-term solution is established, allowing eligible operators to continue using the current pathways.
The proposed guidance will form Annex B to Advisory Circular AC 101-06 and build on the pathways introduced through the trial.

items.title: Early tests show fiber-optic sensors could flag cracks in nuclear fuel storage canisters
items.originalTitle: Early tests show fiber-optic sensors could flag cracks in nuclear fuel storage canisters
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh Swanson School of Engineering have partnered with Pittsburgh startup Sensible Photonics, co-founded by Pitt professor Paul Ohodnicki, to develop a fiber-optic ultrasonic acoustic-sensing system that can detect corrosion and cracking in steel nuclear fuel storage canisters. From Sept. 8 to 11, the Pitt team of Ohodnicki, Khurram Naeem and Yang-Duan Su conducted field testing of an early concept of the technology at the Idaho National Laboratory (INL) in Idaho Falls, Idaho.

evidenceRecords.text: Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh Swanson School of Engineering have partnered with Pittsburgh startup Sensible Photonics, co-founded by Pitt professor Paul Ohodnicki, to develop a fiber-optic ultrasonic acoustic-sensing system that can detect corrosion and cracking in steel nuclear fuel storage canisters.

From Sept. 8 to 11, the Pitt team of Ohodnicki, Khurram Naeem and Yang-Duan Su conducted field testing of an early concept of the technology at the Idaho National Laboratory (INL) in Idaho Falls, Idaho.
The tests demonstrated the feasibility of the system, which has the potential to keep nuclear energy plants and surrounding communities safer.

"People tend to think about fiber optics as a way to produce faster internet speeds, but it can be used to continuously monitor everything from bridges to batteries to nuclear waste," said Naeem, technical lead on the demonstrations and a research assistant professor in mechanical engineering and materials science.
"We have developed and now demonstrated a system that can detect signals above 100 kilohertz, which can be retrofitted onto casks used to hold spent nuclear fuel.
Most conventional counterpart systems have a 20-kilohertz capability."
At nuclear reactor sites, spent fuel is cooled in water and then sealed into steel canisters, which are encased in concrete casks that can remain onsite for decades.
Even after cooling, spent fuel generates heat, so the casks include vents.
"Many nuclear energy plants are near coasts, and these vents can let in salty air that can corrode the steel, creating cracks that could compromise the canister's integrity," said Su (Ph.D.
MEMS), a postdoctoral research associate.
The fiber-optic sensing was developed to monitor the sound produced if a steel canister began corroding and cracking, alerting officials before a dangerous accident occurred.

"At the INL, we deployed the fibers outside a mock canister using different configurations to demonstrate the sensors could detect different magnitudes of acoustic vibration, validating the sensitivity of the sensor," said Su.

The annual challenge, often called a hackathon, is an intensive, collaborative problem-solving experience where participants tackle real-world challenges created by NASA subject matter experts.

This year’s Space Apps Challenge collectively supports three major focus areas: returning humans to the Moon, preparing for missions deeper into the solar system, and expanding understanding of the universe.
Students, scientists, engineers, designers, storytellers, technologists, and space enthusiasts of all ages and experience levels can contribute their skills.

“At NASA, science is for everyone, and we’re inviting the next generation to help tackle some of humanity’s most critical challenges in space through the NASA Space Apps Challenge,” said Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters in Washington.

“Everything in NASA Science is interconnected, and this year, students from around the world can use NASA’s powerful data sets to help us build the ultimate interplanetary survival guide – supporting the science that will enable astronauts to thrive on the Moon and, eventually, Mars, while also inspiring ideas that improve everyday life on Earth and in space for the benefit of all.” Supporting lunar exploration, Artemis planning NASA continues to advance plans for a sustained human presence on the Moon through the Artemis program and Moon Base.
Several of this year’s Space Apps challenges relate to analytical tools, operational considerations, and human‑system needs relevant to lunar missions.
Registration is available at the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

items.originalTitle: What is Starshield, and who limited Ukraine’s access to it?
items.summary: Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service, to fight Russia. Ukraine’s military Starshield satellite connection has been restored, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defence source says, just days after the United States reportedly restricted the service. Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s internet service, Starlink, to provide intelligence amid its war with Russia. Ukraine’s military relies on Starshield, especially to guide its drones, on which it relies heavily to attack Russia.

Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service, to fight Russia.
Ukraine’s military Starshield satellite connection has been restored, a Ukrainian Ministry of Defence source says, just days after the United States reportedly restricted the service.
Ukraine relies on Starshield, the military-grade version of SpaceX’s internet service, Starlink, to provide intelligence amid its war with Russia.
Ukraine’s military relies on Starshield, especially to guide its drones, on which it relies heavily to attack Russia.
On Tuesday, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions.
This came in the wake of heavy Russian strikes, which hit the country with more than 100 drones and five ballistic missiles, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.

Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”
Last year, Starlink cut off access for Russian troops who were covertly using the service on the battlefront in Ukraine.

items.title: Why Open-Weight AI Matters
items.originalTitle: Why Open-Weight AI Matters
items.summary: That difference is what drives deployment. “In practice, the small and mid-sized open-weight models are the ones technically sophisticated users — engineers mostly — download and run on their own hardware, and the motivation is overwhelmingly cost,” Roddy said. “Some run locally to keep prompt data private, and that matters in regulated industries, but token economics is by far the bigger driver today.” Roddy expects the closed-model vendors to come after that local token volume.

evidenceRecords.text: That difference is what drives deployment. “In practice, the small and mid-sized open-weight models are the ones technically sophisticated users — engineers mostly — download and run on their own hardware, and the motivation is overwhelmingly cost,” Roddy said. “Some run locally to keep prompt data private, and that matters in regulated industries, but token economics is by far the bigger driver today.”
Roddy expects the closed-model vendors to come after that local token volume.

“It would surprise no one to see the large private model companies orchestrate split deployments — a midsize front-end model running on the user’s own hardware, with the large model in the cloud handling what the local model can’t.
Those big model companies absolutely do not want some other vendor or other model running locally to become the front door that gates access to the big paid model in the cloud.

The pricing incentive is obvious — offer dramatically cheaper (maybe free) tokens for the ones the user generates on their own machine, on their own electricity, and cut the data center rental bill enormously.
When an offhand tweet (Sam Altman, April 2025) says that the cost of users typing ‘thank you’ runs to tens of millions of dollars, the pressure to offload inference to the edge is not subtle.”

Nordita, the Nordic Institute for Theoretical Physics in Stockholm, will play a key role in this initiative supporting the leadership of the Nordic-Baltic Quantum Academy — one of the EQA’s six regional quantum academies.
Supported by a total budget of €19.8 million over 48 months (with 50% of it directly financed by the European Union) the EQA is the largest community in quantum workforce development to date.
The project unites 73 partners and over 100 affiliates spanning 23 European countries.

These efforts align as well with the newly published Swedish strategy for quantum technology, in which Nordic Quantum — a network coordinated from Nordita — is highlighted as an example of collaboration in the Nordic region.
The fact that Sweden via Nordita and Stockholm University enters the newly established European Skills Academy is highly welcome, notes Director General and Sweden’s Science Council Katarina Bjelke.
Now, through the Nordic-Baltic Quantum Academy, Nordita ensures that Sweden and its neighbors remain deeply integrated into the European quantum landscape.

By expanding access to experimental and digital infrastructures, the EQA will serve as Europe’s anchor for quantum skills, ensuring global leadership in a domain critical for future innovation and security.
